entries.ee4315bcb5d3f88b7f723956f1c263ad7ae3a7bc: <div sID="gen5068" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="20" osisID="Judg.20" sID="Judg.20"/> <div eID="gen5068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5069" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5070" type="x-p"/> Into the book of the wars of the Lord the story of this chapter must be brought, but it looks as sad and uncomfortable as any article in all that history; for there is nothing in it that looks in the least bright or pleasant but the pious zeal of Israel against the wickedness of the men of Gibeah, which made it on their side a just and holy war; but otherwise the obstinacy of the Benjamites in protecting their criminals, which was the foundation of the war, the vast loss which the Israelites sustained in carrying on the war, and (though the righteous cause was victorious at last) the issuing of the war in the almost utter extirpation of the tribe of Benjamin, make it, from first to last, melancholy. And yet this happened soon after the glorious settlement of Israel in the land of promise, upon which one would have expected every thing to be prosperous and serene. In this chapter we have, I. The Levite's cause heard in a general convention of the tribes, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.1-Judg.20.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. A unanimous resolve to avenge his quarrel upon the men of Gibeah, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.8-Judg.20.11">ver. 8-11</reference>. III. The Benjamites appearing in defence of the criminals, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.12-Judg.20.17">ver. 12-17</reference>. IV. The defeat of Israel in the first and second day's battle, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.18-Judg.20.25">ver. 18-25</reference>. V. Their humbling themselves before God upon that occasion, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.26-Judg.20.28">ver. 26-28</reference>. VI. The total rout they gave the Benjamites in the third engagement, by a stratagem, by which they were all cut off, except 600 men, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.29-Judg.20.48">ver. 29-48</reference>. And all this the effect of the indignities done to one poor Levite and his wife; so little do those that do iniquity consider what will be the end thereof.
entries.1f33bbd21e56d4384e79fef014e58f4b6bb755b0: <div eID="gen5070" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5069" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Combination Against Gibeah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1410.)</title> <div sID="gen5071" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then all the children of Israel went out, and the congregation was gathered together as one man, from Dan even to Beer-sheba, with the land of Gilead, unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in Mizpeh. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the chief of all the people, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of all the tribes of Israel, presented themselves in the assembly of the people of God, four hundred thousand footmen that drew sword. <hi type="super">3</hi> (Now the children of Benjamin heard that the children of Israel were gone up to Mizpeh.) Then said the children of Israel, Tell <hi type="italic">us,</hi> how was this wickedness? <hi type="super">4</hi> And the Levite, the husband of the woman that was slain, answered and said, I came into Gibeah that <hi type="italic">belongeth</hi> to Benjamin, I and my concubine, to lodge. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the men of Gibeah rose against me, and beset the house round about upon me by night, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thought to have slain me: and my concubine have they forced, that she is dead. <hi type="super">6</hi> And I took my concubine, and cut her in pieces, and sent her throughout all the country of the inheritance of Israel: for they have committed lewdness and folly in Israel. <hi type="super">7</hi> Behold, ye <hi type="italic">are</hi> all children of Israel; give here your advice and counsel. <hi type="super">8</hi> And all the people arose as one man, saying, We will not any <hi type="italic">of us</hi> go to his tent, neither will we any <hi type="italic">of us</hi> turn into his house. <hi type="super">9</hi> But now this <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the thing which we will do to Gibeah; <hi type="italic">we will go up</hi> by lot against it; <hi type="super">10</hi> And we will take ten men of a hundred throughout all the tribes of Israel, and a hundred of a thousand, and a thousand out of ten thousand, to fetch victual for the people, that they may do, when they come to Gibeah of Benjamin, according to all the folly that they have wrought in Israel. <hi type="super">11</hi> So all the men of Israel were gathered against the city, knit together as one man. <div eID="gen5071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5072" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A general meeting of all the congregation of Israel to examine the matter concerning the Levite's concubine, and to consider what was to be done upon it, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.1-Judg.20.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. It does not appear that they were summoned by the authority of any one common head, but they came together by the consent and agreement, as it were, of one common heart, fired with a holy zeal for the honour of God and Israel. 1. The place of their meeting was <hi type="italic">Mizpeh;</hi> they gathered together unto the Lord there, for Mizpeh was so very near to Shiloh that their encampment might very well be supposed to reach from Mizpeh to Shiloh. Shiloh was a small town, and therefore, when there was a general meeting of the people to represent themselves before God, they chose Mizpeh for their head-quarters, which was the next adjoining city of note, perhaps because they were not willing to give that trouble to Shiloh which so great an assembly would occasion, it being the resident of the priests that attended the tabernacle. 2. The persons that met were all Israel, from Dan (the city very lately so called, <reference osisRef="Judg.18.29">ch. xviii. 29</reference>) in the north to Beersheba in the south, with the land of Gilead (that is, the tribes on the other side Jordan), all <hi type="italic">as one man,</hi> so unanimous were they in their concern for the public good. Here was an assembly of the people of God, not a convocation of the Levites and priests, though a Levite was the person principally concerned in the cause, but an assembly of the people, to whom the Levite referred himself with an <hi type="italic">Appello populum—I appeal to the people.</hi> The <hi type="italic">people of God were</hi> 400,000 <hi type="italic">footmen that drew the sword,</hi> that is, were armed and disciplined, and fit for service, and some of them perhaps such as had <hi type="italic">known the wars of Canaan,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.3.1">ch. iii. 1</reference>. In this assembly of all Israel, the chief (or corners) of the people (for rulers are the corner-stones of the people, that keep all together) presented themselves as the representatives of the rest. They rendered themselves at their respective posts, at the head of the thousands and hundreds, the fifties and tens, over which they presided; for so much order and government, we may suppose, at least, they had among them, though they had no general or commander-in-chief. So that here was, (1.) A general congress of the states for counsel. The chief of the people presented themselves, to lead and direct in this affair. (2.) A general rendezvous of the militia for action, all that drew sword and were men of war (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.17">v. 17</reference>), not hirelings nor pressed men, but the best freeholders, that went at their own charge. Israel were above 600,000 when they came into Canaan, and we have reason to think they were at this time much increased, rather than diminished; but then all between twenty and sixty were military men, now we may suppose more than the one half exempted from bearing arms to cultivate the land; so that these were as the trained bands. The militia of the two tribes and a half were 40,000 (<reference osisRef="Josh.4.13">Josh. iv. 13</reference>), but the tribes were many more. <div eID="gen5072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5073" type="x-p"/> II. Notice given to the tribe of Benjamin of this meeting (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">They heard that the children of Israel had gone up to Mizpeh.</hi> Probably they had a legal summons sent them to appear with their brethren, that the cause might be fairly debated, before any resolutions were taken up upon it, and so the mischiefs that followed would have been happily prevented; but the notice they had of this meeting rather hardened and exasperated them than awakened them to think of the things that belonged to their peace and honour. <div eID="gen5073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5074" type="x-p"/> III. A solemn examination of the crime charged upon the men of Gibeah. A very horrid representation of it had been made by the report of the messengers that were sent to call them together, but it was fit it should be more closely enquired into, because such things are often made worse than really they were; a committee therefore was appointed to examine the witnesses (upon oath, no doubt) and to report the matter. It is only the testimony of the Levite himself that is here recorded, but it is probable his servant, and the old man, were examined, and gave in their testimony, for that more than one were examined appears by the original (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.3">v. 3</reference>), which is, <hi type="italic">Tell you us;</hi> and the law was that none should be put to death, much less so many, upon the testimony of one witness only. The Levite gives a particular account of the matter: that he came into Gibeah only as a traveller to lodge there, not giving the least shadow of suspicion that he designed them any ill turn (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.4">v. 4</reference>), and that the men of Gibeah, even those that were of substance among them, that should have been a protection to the stranger within their gates, riotously set upon the house where he lodged, and <hi type="italic">thought to slay him;</hi> he could not, for shame relate the demand which they, without shame, made, <reference osisRef="Judg.19.22">ch. xix. 22</reference>. They declared their sin as Sodom, even the sin of Sodom, but his modesty would not suffer him to repeat it; it was sufficient to say they would have slain him, for he would rather have been slain than have submitted to their villany; and, if they had got him into their hands, they would have abused him to death, witness what they had done to his concubine: They have <hi type="italic">forced her that she is dead,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.20.5">v. 5</reference>. And, to excite in his countrymen an indignation at this wickedness, he had sent pieces of the mangled body to all the tribes, which had fetched them together to bear their testimony against the <hi type="italic">lewdness and folly committed in Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.20.6">v. 6</reference>. All lewdness is folly, but especially lewdness in Israel. For those to defile their own bodies who have the honourable seal of the covenant in their flesh, for those to defy the divine vengeance to whom it is so clearly revealed from heaven—Nabal is their name, and folly is with them. He concludes his declaration with an appeal to the judgment of the court (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">You are all children of Israel,</hi> and therefore you <hi type="italic">know law and judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.1.13">Esth. i. 13</reference>. "You are a holy people to God, and have a dread of every thing which will dishonour God and defile the land; you are of the same community, members of the same body, and therefore likely to feel from the distempers of it; you are children of Israel, that ought to take particular care of the Levites, God's tribe, among you, and therefore give your advice and counsel what is to be done." <div eID="gen5074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5075" type="x-p"/> IV. The resolution they came to hereupon, which was that, being now together, they would not disperse till they had seen vengeance taken upon this wicked city, which was the reproach and scandal of their nation. Observe, 1. Their zeal against the lewdness that was committed. They would not return to their houses, how much soever their families and their affairs at home wanted them, till they had vindicated the honour of God and Israel, and recovered with their swords, if it could not be had otherwise, that satisfaction for the crime which the justice of the nation called for, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.8">v. 8</reference>. By this they showed themselves children of Israel indeed, that they preferred the public interest before their private concerns. 2. Their prudence in sending out a considerable body of their forces to fetch provisions for the rest, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.9-Judg.20.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. One of ten, and he chosen by lot, 40,000 in all, must go to their respective countries, whence they came, to fetch bread and other necessaries for the subsistence of this great army; for when they came from home they took with them provisions only for a journey to Mizpeh, not for an encampment (which might prove long) before Gibeah. This was to prevent their scattering to forage for themselves, for, if they had done this, it would have been hard to get them all together again, especially all in so good a mind. Note, When there appears in people a pious zeal for any good work it is best to strike while the iron is hot, for such zeal is apt to cool quickly if the prosecution of the work be delayed. Let it never be said that we left that good work to be done to-morrow which we could as well have done to-day. 3. Their unanimity in these counsels, and the execution of them. The resolution was voted, <hi type="italic">Nemine contradicente—Without a dissenting voice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.8">v. 8</reference>); it was one and all; and, when it was put in execution, they were <hi type="italic">knit together as one man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.20.11">v. 11</reference>. This was their glory and strength, that the several tribes had no separate interests when the common good was concerned.
entries.bb75b97e8094aff49e7d196ece285421d70be5c3: <div eID="gen5075" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The War with the Benjamites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1410.)</title> <div sID="gen5076" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> And the tribes of Israel sent men through all the tribe of Benjamin, saying, What wickedness <hi type="italic">is</hi> this that is done among you? <hi type="super">13</hi> Now therefore deliver <hi type="italic">us</hi> the men, the children of Belial, which <hi type="italic">are</hi> in Gibeah, that we may put them to death, and put away evil from Israel. But the children of Benjamin would not hearken to the voice of their brethren the children of Israel: <hi type="super">14</hi> But the children of Benjamin gathered themselves together out of the cities unto Gibeah, to go out to battle against the children of Israel. <hi type="super">15</hi> And the children of Benjamin were numbered at that time out of the cities twenty and six thousand men that drew sword, beside the inhabitants of Gibeah, which were numbered seven hundred chosen men. <hi type="super">16</hi> Among all this people <hi type="italic">there were</hi> seven hundred chosen men lefthanded; every one could sling stones at a hair <hi type="italic">breadth,</hi> and not miss. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the men of Israel, beside Benjamin, were numbered four hundred thousand men that drew sword: all these <hi type="italic">were</hi> men of war. <div eID="gen5076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5077" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The fair and just demand which the tribes of Israel, now encamped, sent to the tribe of Benjamin, to deliver up the malefactors of Gibeah to justice, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.12-Judg.20.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. If the tribe of Benjamin had come up, as they ought to have done, to the assembly, and agreed with them in their resolution, there would have been none to deal with but the men of Gibeah only, but they, by their absence, taking part with the criminals, application must be made to them all. The Israelites were zealous against the wickedness that was committed, yet they were discreet in their zeal, and did not think it would justify them in falling upon the whole tribe of Benjamin unless they, by refusing to give up the criminals, and protecting them against justice, should make themselves guilty, <hi type="italic">ex post facto</hi>—<hi type="italic">as accessaries after the fact.</hi> They desire them to consider how great the wickedness was that was committed (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.12">v. 12</reference>), and that it was done among them: and how necessary it was therefore that they should either punish the malefactors with death themselves, according to the law of Moses, or deliver them up to the general assembly, to be so much the more publicly and solemnly punished, that evil might be put away from Israel, the national guilt removed, the infection stopped by cutting off the gangrened part, and national judgments prevented; for the sin was so very like that of the Sodomites that they might justly fear, if they did not punish it, God would rain hail from heaven upon them, as he did, not only upon Sodom, but the neighbouring cities. If the Israelites had not made this reasonable demand, they would have had much more reason to lament the following desolations of Benjamin. All methods of accommodation must be used before we go to war or go to law. The demand was like that of Joab's to Abel, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.20-2Sam.20.21">2 Sam. xx. 20, 21</reference>. "Only deliver up the traitor, and we will lay down our arms." On these terms, and no other, God will be at peace with us, that we part with our sins, that we mortify and crucify our lusts, and then all shall be well; his anger will be turned away. <div eID="gen5077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5078" type="x-p"/> II. The wretched obstinacy and perverseness of the men of Benjamin, who seem to have been as unanimous and zealous in their resolutions to stand by the criminals as the rest of the tribes were to punish them, so little sense had they of their honour, duty, and interest. 1. They were so prodigiously vile as to patronise the wickedness that was committed: They <hi type="italic">would not hearken to the voice of their brethren</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.13">v. 13</reference>), either because those of that tribe were generally more vicious and debauched at this time than the rest of the tribes, and therefore would not bear to have that punished in others of which they knew themselves guilty (some of the most fruitful and pleasant parts of Canaan fell to the lot of this tribe; their land, like that of Sodom, was <hi type="italic">as the garden of the Lord,</hi> which perhaps helped to make the inhabitants, like the men of Sodom, wicked, and <hi type="italic">sinners before the Lord exceedingly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.13.10">Gen. xiii. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.13.13">13</reference>), or because (as bishop Patrick suggests) they took it ill that the other tribes should meddle with their concerns; they would not do that which they knew was their duty because they were reminded of it by their brethren, by whom they scorned to be taught and controlled. If there were any wise men among them that would have complied with the demand made, yet they were overpowered by the majority, who thus made the crime of the men of Gibeah their own. Thus we have <hi type="italic">fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness</hi> if we say <hi type="italic">A confederacy</hi> with those that have, and make ourselves guilty of other men's sins by countenancing and defending them. It seems there is no cause so bad but it will find some patrons, some advocates, to appear for it; but <hi type="italic">woe be to those by whom such offences come.</hi> Those will have a great deal to answer for that obstruct the course of necessary justice, and strengthen the hands of the wicked, by saying, <hi type="italic">O wicked man! thou shalt not die.</hi> <div eID="gen5078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5079" type="x-p"/> 2. They were so prodigiously vain and presumptuous as to make head against the united force of all Israel. Never, surely, were men so wretchedly infatuated as they were when they took up arms in opposition, (1.) To so good a cause as Israel had. How could they expect to prosper when they fought against justice, and consequently against the just God himself, against those that had the high priest and the divine oracle on their side, and so acted in downright rebellion against the sacred and supreme authority of the nation. (2.) To so great a force as Israel had. The disproportion of their numbers was much greater than that, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.31-Luke.14.32">Luke xiv. 31, 32</reference>, where he that had but 10,000 durst not meet him that came against him with 20,000, and therefore desired conditions of peace. There the enemy was but two to one, here above fifteen to one; yet they despised conditions of peace. All the forces they could bring into the field were but 26,000 men, besides 700 men of Gibeah (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.15">v. 15</reference>); yet with these they will dare to face 400,000 men of Israel, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.17">v. 17</reference>. Thus sinners are infatuated to their own ruin, and provoke him to jealousy who is infinitely stronger than they, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.22">1 Cor. x. 22</reference>. But it should seem they depended upon the skill of their men to make up what was wanting in numbers, especially a regiment of slingers, 700 men, who, though left-handed, were so dexterous at slinging stones that they would not be a hair's breadth beside their mark, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.16">v. 16</reference>. But these good marksmen were very much out in their aim when they espoused this bad cause. <hi type="italic">Benjamin</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">the son of the right hand,</hi> yet we find his posterity left-handed.
entries.c672ab31374d00edae7100fb478c8a42e539c93d: <div eID="gen5079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5080" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> And the children of Israel arose, and went up to the house of God, and asked counsel of God, and said, Which of us shall go up first to the battle against the children of Benjamin? And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said, Judah <hi type="italic">shall go up</hi> first. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the children of Israel rose up in the morning, and encamped against Gibeah. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the men of Israel went out to battle against Benjamin; and the men of Israel put themselves in array to fight against them at Gibeah. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the children of Benjamin came forth out of Gibeah, and destroyed down to the ground of the Israelites that day twenty and two thousand men. <hi type="super">22</hi> And the people the men of Israel encouraged themselves, and set their battle again in array in the place where they put themselves in array the first day.   23 (And the children of Israel went up and wept before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> until even, and asked counsel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, Shall I go up again to battle against the children of Benjamin my brother? And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said, Go up against him.) <hi type="super">24</hi> And the children of Israel came near against the children of Benjamin the second day. <hi type="super">25</hi> And Benjamin went forth against them out of Gibeah the second day, and destroyed down to the ground of the children of Israel again eighteen thousand men; all these drew the sword. <div eID="gen5080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5081" type="x-p"/> We have here the defeat of the men of Israel in their first and second battle with the Benjamites. <div eID="gen5081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5082" type="x-p"/> I. Before their first engagement they asked counsel of God concerning the order of their battle and were directed, and yet they were sorely beaten. They did not think it was proper to ask of God whether they should go up at all against Benjamin (the case was plain enough, the men of Gibeah must be punished for their wickedness, and Israel must inflict the punishment or it will not be done), but "Who shall go first?" (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.18">v. 18</reference>), that is, "Who shall be general of our army?" for, which soever tribe was appointed to go first, the prince of that tribe must be looked upon as commander-in-chief of the whole body. For, if they had meant it of the order of their march only, it would have been proper to ask, "Who shall go next?" and then, "Who next?" But, if they know that Judah must go first, they know they must all observe the orders of the prince of that tribe. This honour was done to Judah because our Lord Jesus was to spring from that tribe, who was in all things to have the pre-eminence. The tribe that went up first had the most honourable post, but withal the most dangerous, and probably lost most in the engagement. Who would strive for precedency that sees the peril of it? Yet though Judah, that strong and valiant tribe, goes up first, and all the tribes of Israel attend them, <hi type="italic">little Benjamin</hi> (so he is called, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.27">Ps. lxviii. 27</reference>), is too hard for them all. The whole army lays siege to Gibeah, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.19">v. 19</reference>. The Benjamites advance to raise the siege, and the army prepares to give them a warm reception, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.20">v. 20</reference>. But between the Benjamites that attacked them in the front with incredible fury, and the men of Gibeah that sallied out upon their rear, they were put into confusion and lost 22,000 men, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.21">v. 21</reference>. Here were no prisoners taken, for there was no quarter given, but all put to the sword. <div eID="gen5082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5083" type="x-p"/> II. Before their second engagement they again <hi type="italic">asked counsel of God,</hi> and more solemnly than before; for they <hi type="italic">wept before the Lord until evening</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.23">v. 23</reference>), lamenting the loss of so many brave men, especially as it was a token of God's displeasure and would give occasion to the Benjamites to triumph in the success of their wickedness. Also at this time they did not ask who should go up first, but whether they should go up at all. The intimate a reason why they should scruple to do it, especially now that Providence had frowned upon them, because Benjamin was their brother, and a readiness to lay down their arms if God should so order them. God bade them go up; he allowed the attempt, for, though Benjamin was their brother, he was a gangrened member of their body and must be cut off. Upon this they encouraged themselves, perhaps more in their own strength than in the divine commission, and made a second attempt upon the forces of the rebels, in the same place where the former battle was fought (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.22">v. 22</reference>), with the hope of retrieving their credit upon the same spot of ground where they had lost it, which they would not superstitiously change, as if there were any thing unlucky in the place. But they were this second time repulsed, with the loss of 18,000 men, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.25">v. 25</reference>. The former day's loss and this amounted to 40,000, which was just a tenth part of the whole army, and the same number that they had drawn out by lot to fetch victuals, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.10">v. 10</reference>. They decimated themselves for that service, and now God again decimated them for the slaughter. But what shall we say to these things, that so just and honourable a cause should thus be put to the worst once and again? Were they not fighting God's battle against sin? Had they not his commission? What, and yet miscarry thus! 1. God's judgments are a great deep, and his way is in the sea. <hi type="italic">Clouds and darkness are</hi> often <hi type="italic">round about</hi> him, <hi type="italic">but judgment and justice are</hi> always <hi type="italic">the habitation of his throne.</hi> We may be sure of the righteousness, when we cannot see the reasons, of God's proceedings. 2. God would hereby show them, and us in them, that <hi type="italic">the race is not to the swift nor the battle to the strong,</hi> that we are not to confide in numbers, which perhaps the Israelites did with too much assurance. We must never lay the weight on an arm of flesh, which only the Rock of ages will bear. 3. God designed hereby to correct Israel for their sins. They did well to show such a zeal against the wickedness of Gibeah: but <hi type="italic">were there not with them, even with them, sins against the Lord their God?</hi> Those must be made to know their own iniquity that are forward in condemning the iniquity of others. Some think it was a rebuke to them for not witnessing against the idolatry of Micah and the Danites, by which their religion was corrupted, as they now did against the lewdness of Gibeah and the Benjamites, by which the public peace was disturbed, though God had particularly ordered them to levy war upon idolaters, <reference osisRef="Deut.13.12-Deut.13.18">Deut. xiii. 12</reference>, &c. 4. God would hereby teach us not to think it strange if a good cause should suffer defeat for a while, nor to judge of the merits of it by the success of it. The interest of grace in the heart, and of religion in the world, may be foiled, and suffer great loss, and seem to be quite run down, but judgment will be brought forth to victory at last. <hi type="italic">Vincimur in prælio, sed non in bello—We are foiled in a battle, but not in the whole campaign.</hi> Right may fall, but it shall arise.
entries.33d39e4c8f918e2b5a125e80cfc2c3fa028a4d4e: <div eID="gen5083" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Defeat of the Benjamites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1410.)</title> <div sID="gen5084" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> Then all the children of Israel, and all the people, went up, and came unto the house of God, and wept, and sat there before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and fasted that day until even, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">27</hi> And the children of Israel enquired of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , (for the ark of the covenant of God <hi type="italic">was</hi> there in those days, <hi type="super">28</hi> And Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, stood before it in those days,) saying, Shall I yet again go out to battle against the children of Benjamin my brother, or shall I cease? And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said, Go up; for to morrow I will deliver them into thine hand. <hi type="super">29</hi> And Israel set liers in wait round about Gibeah. <hi type="super">30</hi> And the children of Israel went up against the children of Benjamin on the third day, and put themselves in array against Gibeah, as at other times. <hi type="super">31</hi> And the children of Benjamin went out against the people, <hi type="italic">and</hi> were drawn away from the city; and they began to smite of the people, <hi type="italic">and</hi> kill, as at other times, in the highways, of which one goeth up to the house of God, and the other to Gibeah in the field, about thirty men of Israel. <hi type="super">32</hi> And the children of Benjamin said, They <hi type="italic">are</hi> smitten down before us, as at the first. But the children of Israel said, Let us flee, and draw them from the city unto the highways. <hi type="super">33</hi> And all the men of Israel rose up out of their place, and put themselves in array at Baal-tamar: and the liers in wait of Israel came forth out of their places, <hi type="italic">even</hi> out of the meadows of Gibeah. <hi type="super">34</hi> And there came against Gibeah ten thousand chosen men out of all Israel, and the battle was sore: but they knew not that evil <hi type="italic">was</hi> near them. <hi type="super">35</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> smote Benjamin before Israel: and the children of Israel destroyed of the Benjamites that day twenty and five thousand and a hundred men: all these drew the sword. <hi type="super">36</hi> So the children of Benjamin saw that they were smitten: for the men of Israel gave place to the Benjamites, because they trusted unto the liers in wait which they had set beside Gibeah. <hi type="super">37</hi> And the liers in wait hasted, and rushed upon Gibeah; and the liers in wait drew <hi type="italic">themselves</hi> along, and smote all the city with the edge of the sword. <hi type="super">38</hi> Now there was an appointed sign between the men of Israel and the liers in wait, that they should make a great flame with smoke rise up out of the city. <hi type="super">39</hi> And when the men of Israel retired in the battle, Benjamin began to smite <hi type="italic">and</hi> kill of the men of Israel about thirty persons: for they said, Surely they are smitten down before us, as <hi type="italic">in</hi> the first battle. <hi type="super">40</hi> But when the flame began to arise up out of the city with a pillar of smoke, the Benjamites looked behind them, and, behold, the flame of the city ascended up to heaven. <hi type="super">41</hi> And when the men of Israel turned again, the men of Benjamin were amazed: for they saw that evil was come upon them. <hi type="super">42</hi> Therefore they turned <hi type="italic">their backs</hi> before the men of Israel unto the way of the wilderness; but the battle overtook them; and them which <hi type="italic">came</hi> out of the cities they destroyed in the midst of them. <hi type="super">43</hi> <hi type="italic">Thus</hi> they inclosed the Benjamites round about, <hi type="italic">and</hi> chased them, <hi type="italic">and</hi> trode them down with ease over against Gibeah toward the sunrising. <hi type="super">44</hi> And there fell of Benjamin eighteen thousand men; all these <hi type="italic">were</hi> men of valour. <hi type="super">45</hi> And they turned and fled toward the wilderness unto the rock of Rimmon: and they gleaned of them in the highways five thousand men; and pursued hard after them unto Gidom, and slew two thousand men of them. <hi type="super">46</hi> So that all which fell that day of Benjamin were twenty and five thousand men that drew the sword; all these <hi type="italic">were</hi> men of valour. <hi type="super">47</hi> But six hundred men turned and fled to the wilderness unto the rock Rimmon, and abode in the rock Rimmon four months. <hi type="super">48</hi> And the men of Israel turned again upon the children of Benjamin, and smote them with the edge of the sword, as well the men of <hi type="italic">every</hi> city, as the beast, and all that came to hand: also they set on fire all the cities that they came to. <div eID="gen5084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5085" type="x-p"/> We have here a full account of the complete victory which the Israelites obtained over the Benjamites in the third engagement: the righteous cause was victorious at last, when the managers of it amended what had been amiss; for, when a good cause suffers, it is for want of good management. Observe then how the victory was obtained, and how it was pursued. <div eID="gen5085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5086" type="x-p"/> I. How the victory was obtained. Two things they had trusted too much to in the former engagements—the goodness of their cause and the superiority of their numbers. It was true that they had both right and strength on their side, which were great advantages; but they depended too much upon them, to the neglect of those duties to which now, this third time, when they see their error, they apply themselves. <div eID="gen5086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5087" type="x-p"/> 1. They were previously so confident of the goodness of their cause that they thought it needless to address themselves to God for his presence and blessing. They took it for granted that God would bless them, nay, perhaps they concluded that he owed them his favour, and could not in justice withhold it, since it was in defence of virtue that they appeared and took up arms. But God having shown them that he was under no obligation to prosper their enterprise, that he neither needed them nor was tied to them, that they were more indebted to him for the honour of being ministers of his justice than he to them for the service, now they became humble petitioners for success. Before they only consulted God's oracle, <hi type="italic">Who shall go up first?</hi> And, <hi type="italic">Shall we go up?</hi> But now they implored his favour, fasted and prayed, and <hi type="italic">offered burnt-offerings and peace-offerings</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.26">v. 26</reference>), to make an atonement for sin and an acknowledgment of their dependence upon God, and as an expression of their desire towards him. We cannot expect the presence of God with us, unless we thus seek it in the way he has appointed. And when they were in this frame, and thus sought the Lord, then he not only ordered them to go up against the Benjamites the third time, but gave them a promise of victory: <hi type="italic">Tomorrow I will deliver them into thy hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.20.28">v. 28</reference>. <div eID="gen5087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5088" type="x-p"/> 2. They were previously so confident of the greatness of their strength that they thought it needless to use any art, to lay any ambush, or form a stratagem, not doubting but to conquer purely by a strong hand; but now they saw it was requisite to use some policy, as if they had an enemy to deal with them that had been superior in number; accordingly, they set <hi type="italic">liers in wait</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.29">v. 29</reference>), and gained their point, as their fathers did before Ai (<reference osisRef="Josh.8.1-Josh.8.35">Josh. viii.</reference>), stratagems of that kind being most likely to take effect after a previous defeat, which has flushed the enemy, and made the pretended flight the less suspected. The management of this artifice is here very largely described. The assurance God had given them of success in this day's action, instead of making them remiss and presumptuous, set all heads and hands on work for the effecting of what God had promised. <div eID="gen5088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5089" type="x-p"/> (1.) Observe the method they took. The body of the army faced the city of Gibeah, as they had done before, advancing towards the gates, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.30">v. 30</reference>. The Benjamites, the body of whose army was now quartered at Gibeah, sallied out upon them, and charged them with great bravery. The besiegers gave back, retired with precipitation, as if their hearts failed them upon the sight of the Benjamites, which they were willing to believe, proudly imagining that by their former success they had made themselves very formidable. Some loss the Israelites sustained in this counterfeit flight, about thirty men being cut off in their rear, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.31">v. 31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.39">39</reference>. But, when the Benjamites were all drawn out of the city, the ambush seized the city (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.37">v. 37</reference>), gave a signal to the body of the army (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.38">v. 38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.40">40</reference>), which immediately turned upon them (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.41">v. 41</reference>), and, it should seem, another considerable party that was posted at Baal-tamar came upon them at the same time (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.33">v. 33</reference>); so that the Benjamites were quite surrounded, which put them into the greatest consternation that could be. A sense of guilt now disheartened them, and the higher their hopes had been raised the more grievous was this confusion. At first <hi type="italic">the battle was sore</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.34">v. 34</reference>), the Benjamites fought with fury; but, when they saw what a snare they were drawn into, they thought one pair of heels (as we say) was worth two pair of hands, and they made the best of their way <hi type="italic">towards the wilderness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.42">v. 42</reference>); but in vain: <hi type="italic">the battle overtook them,</hi> and, to complete their distress, <hi type="italic">those who came out of the cities of Israel,</hi> that waited to see the event of the battle, joined with their pursuers, and helped to cut them off. Every man's hand was against them. <div eID="gen5089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5090" type="x-p"/> (2.) Observe in this story, [1.] That the Benjamites, in the beginning of the battle, were confident that the day was their own: <hi type="italic">They are smitten down before us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.20.32">v. 32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.39">39</reference>. Sometimes God suffers wicked men to be lifted up in successes and hopes, that their fall may be the sorer. See how short their joy is, and their triumphing but for a moment. <hi type="italic">Let not him that girdeth on the harness boast,</hi> except he has reason to boast in God. [2.] Evil was near them and they did not know it, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.34">v. 34</reference>. But (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.41">v. 41</reference>) they saw, when it was too late to prevent it, <hi type="italic">that evil had come upon them.</hi> What evils may at any time be near us we cannot tell, but the less they are feared the heavier they fall. Sinners will not be persuaded to see evil near them, but how dreadful will it be when it comes and there is no escaping! <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.3">1 Thess. v. 3</reference>. [3.] Though the men of Israel played their parts so well in this engagement, yet the victory is ascribed to God (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord smote Benjamin before Israel.</hi> The battle was his, and so was the success. [4.] They <hi type="italic">trode down the men of Benjamin with ease</hi> when God fought against them, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.43">v. 43</reference>. It is an easy thing to trample upon those who have made God their enemy. See <reference osisRef="Mal.4.3">Mal. iv. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen5090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5091" type="x-p"/> II. How the victory was prosecuted and improved in a military execution done upon these sinners against their own souls. 1. Gibeah itself, that nest of lewdness, was destroyed in the first place. The ambush that entered the city by surprise <hi type="italic">drew themselves along,</hi> that is, dispersed themselves into the several parts of it, which they might easily do, now that all the men of war had sallied out and very presumptuously left it defenceless; and they smote all they found, even women and children, <hi type="italic">with the sword</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.37">v. 37</reference>), and set fire to the city, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.40">v. 40</reference>. Sin brings ruin upon cities. 2. The army in the field was quite routed and cut off: 18,000 men of valour lay dead upon the spot, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.44">v. 44</reference>. 3. Those that escaped from the field were pursued, and cut off in their flight, to the number of 7000, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.45">v. 45</reference>. It is to no purpose to think of out-running divine vengeance. <hi type="italic">Evil pursues sinners,</hi> and it will overtake them. 4. Even those that tarried at home were involved in the ruin. They <hi type="italic">let their sword devour for ever,</hi> not considering that <hi type="italic">it would be bitterness in the latter end,</hi> as Abner pleads long after, when he was at the head of an army of Benjamites, probably with an eye to this very story, <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.25-2Sam.2.26">2 Sam. ii. 25, 26</reference>. They put to the sword all that breathed, and set fire to <hi type="italic">all the cities,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.20.48">v. 48</reference>. So that of all the tribe of Benjamin, for aught that appears, there remained none alive but 600 men that took shelter in the rock Rimmon, and lay close there four months, <reference osisRef="Judg.20.47">v. 47</reference>. Now, (1.) It is difficult to justify this severity as it was Israel's act. The whole tribe of Benjamin was culpable; but must they therefore be treated as devoted Canaanites? That it was done in the heat of war, that this was the way of prosecuting victories which the sword of Israel had been accustomed to, that the Israelites were extremely exasperated against the Benjamites for the slaughter they had made among them in the two former engagements, will go but a little way to excuse the cruelty of this execution. It is true they had sworn that whosoever did not come up to Mizpeh should be <hi type="italic">put to death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.21.5">ch. xxi. 5</reference>. But that, if it was a justifiable oath, yet extended only to the men of war; the rest were not expected to come. Yet, (2.) It is easy to justify the hand of God in it. Benjamin had sinned against him, and God had threatened that, if they forgot him, they should <hi type="italic">perish as the nations</hi> that were before them perished (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.20">Deut. viii. 20</reference>), who were all in this manner cut off. (3.) It is easy likewise to improve it for warning against the beginnings of sin: they are <hi type="italic">like the letting forth of water, therefore leave it off before it be meddled with,</hi> for we know not <hi type="italic">what will be in the end thereof.</hi> The eternal ruin of souls will be worse, and more fearful, than all these desolations of a tribe. This affair of Gibeah is twice spoken of by the prophet Hosea as the beginning of the corruption of Israel and a pattern to all that followed (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.9">Hos. ix. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">They have deeply corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah;</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.9">Hos. x. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou hast sinned from the days of Gibeah;</hi> and it is added that <hi type="italic">the battle in Gibeah against the children of iniquity did not</hi> (that is, did not <hi type="italic">at first</hi>) overtake them.  <chapter eID="Judg.20"/> <div eID="gen5091" type="x-p"/>

entries.5e5e7b1477ce59a2612090dcb22921ef8df70b69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2440"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 20</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.20.1-Judg.20.7">Jud 20:1-7</reference>. The Levite, in a General Assembly, Declares His Wrong.</title> <div sID="gen3294" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2440"/><hi type="bold">1-2. all ... the congregation was gathered as one man--</hi>In consequence of the immense sensation the horrid tragedy of Gibeah had produced, a national assembly was convened, at which "the chief of all the people" from all parts of the land, including the eastern tribes, appeared as delegates.<div eID="gen3294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3295" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Mizpeh--</hi>the place of convention (for there were other Mizpehs), was in a town situated on the confines of Judah and Benjamin (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.38">Jos 15:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.18.26">18:26</reference>). Assemblies were frequently held there afterwards (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.11">1Sa 7:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.17">10:17</reference>); and it was but a short distance from Shiloh. The phrase, "unto the Lord," may be taken in its usual sense, as denoting consultation of the oracle. This circumstance, together with the convention being called "the assembly of the people of God," seems to indicate, that amid the excited passions of the nation, those present felt the profound gravity of the occasion and adopted the best means of maintaining a becoming deportment. <div eID="gen3295" type="x-p"/>
entries.523143c3b63c6b7b9cb77885ec4a6f95ad33502d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2441"/><div sID="gen3296" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2441"/><hi type="bold">3. Now the children of Benjamin heard that the children of Israel were gone up to Mizpeh--</hi>Some suppose that Benjamin had been passed over, the crime having been perpetrated within the territory of that tribe [Jud 19:16]; and that, as the concubine's corpse had been divided into twelve pieces [Jud 19:29]--two had been sent to Manasseh, one respectively to the western and eastern divisions. It is more probable that Benjamin had received a formal summons like the other tribes, but chose to treat it with indifference, or haughty disdain. <div eID="gen3296" type="x-p"/>
entries.fbcb106ab69543b4b505fdb6c03b9e547fd3dcfe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2442"/><div sID="gen3297" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2442"/><hi type="bold">4-7. the Levite, the husband of the woman that was slain, answered and said--</hi>The injured husband gave a brief and unvarnished recital of the tragic outrage, from which it appears that force was used, which he could not resist. His testimony was doubtless corroborated by those of his servant and the old Ephraimite. There was no need of strong or highly colored description to work upon the feelings of the audience. The facts spoke for themselves and produced one common sentiment of detestation and vengeance. <div eID="gen3297" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa3601ff253e616108a30f6b24d7eb783269a0fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2443"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.20.8-Judg.20.17">Jud 20:8-17</reference>. Their Decree.</title> <div sID="gen3298" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2443"/><hi type="bold">8-13. all the people arose as one man--</hi>The extraordinary unanimity that prevailed shows, that notwithstanding great disorders had broken out in many parts, the people were sound at the core; and remembering their national covenant with God, they now felt the necessity of wiping out so foul a stain on their character as a people. It was resolved that the inhabitants of Gibeah should be subjected to condign punishment. But the resolutions were conditional. For as the common law of nature and nations requires that an inquiry should be made and satisfaction demanded, before committing an act of hostility or vengeance, messengers were despatched through the whole territory of Benjamin, demanding the immediate surrender or execution of the delinquents. The request was just and reasonable; and by refusing it the Benjamites virtually made themselves a party in the quarrel. It must not be supposed that the people of this tribe were insensible or indifferent to the atrocious character of the crime that had been committed on their soil. But their patriotism or their pride was offended by the hostile demonstration of the other tribes. The passions were inflamed on both sides; but certainly the Benjamites incurred an awful responsibility by the attitude of resistance they assumed. <div eID="gen3298" type="x-p"/>
entries.74bb0dc7653f1088caddf6fd9ae94d20fb77ed7d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2444"/><div sID="gen3299" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2444"/><hi type="bold">14-17. the children of Benjamin gathered themselves together out of the cities unto Gibeah--</hi>Allowing their valor to be ever so great, nothing but blind passion and unbending obstinacy could have impelled them to take the field against their brethren with such a disparity of numbers. <div eID="gen3299" type="x-p"/>
entries.287c039abbeaf2bade8c363638345638cae65780: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2446"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.20.18-Judg.20.28">Jud 20:18-28</reference>. The Israelites Lose Forty Thousand.</title> <div sID="gen3301" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2446"/><hi type="bold">18-28. the children of Israel arose, and went up to the house of God--</hi>This consultation at Shiloh was right. But they ought to have done it at the commencement of their proceedings. Instead of this, all their plans were formed, and never doubting, it would seem, that the war was just and inevitable, the only subject of their inquiry related to the precedency of the tribes--a point which it is likely was discussed in the assembly. Had they asked counsel of God sooner, their expedition would have been conducted on a different principle--most probably by reducing the number of fighting men, as in the case of Gideon's army. As it was, the vast number of volunteers formed an excessive and unwieldy force, unfit for strenuous and united action against a small, compact, and well-directed army. A panic ensued, and the confederate tribes, in two successive engagements, sustained great losses. These repeated disasters (notwithstanding their attack on Benjamin had been divinely authorized) overwhelmed them with shame and sorrow. Led to reflection, they became sensible of their guilt in not repressing their national idolatries, as well as in too proudly relying on their superior numbers and the precipitate rashness of this expedition. Having humbled themselves by prayer and fasting, as well as observed the appointed method of expiating their sins, they were assured of acceptance as well as of victory. The presence and services of Phinehas on this occasion help us to ascertain the chronology thus far, that the date of the occurrence must be fixed shortly after the death of Joshua. <div eID="gen3301" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1de0c213c1952d1da4484d9aec482d5d888b4d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2447"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.20.29-Judg.20.48">Jud 20:29-48</reference>. They Destroy All the Benjamites, Except Six Hundred.</title> <div sID="gen3302" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2447"/><hi type="bold">29-48. And Israel set liers-in-wait round about Gibeah--</hi>A plan was formed of taking that city by stratagem, similar to that employed in the capture of Ai [Jos 8:9]. <div eID="gen3302" type="x-p"/>

entries.e8ad1442f4764cc458603be6a2226b3fb70a5454: <div eID="gen9186" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen9187" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9188" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9188" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9187" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9189" type="x-p"/> The heads of the eleven tribes come before the Lord in Mizpeh, and examine the Levite relative to the murder of his wife, who gives a simple narrative of the whole affair, <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.1-Jdg.20.7">Jdg 20:1-7</reference>. They unanimously resolve to avenge the wrong, and make provision for a campaign against the Benjamites, <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.8-Jdg.20.11">Jdg 20:8-11</reference>. They desire the Benjamites to deliver up the murderers; they refuse, and prepare for battle, having assembled an army of twenty-six thousand seven hundred men, <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.12-Jdg.20.16">Jdg 20:12-16</reference>. The rest of the Israelites amount to four hundred thousand, who, taking counsel of God, agree to send the tribe of Judah against the Benjamites, <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.17">Jdg 20:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.18">Jdg 20:18</reference>. They attack the Benjamites, and are routed with the loss of twenty-two thousand men, <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.19-Jdg.20.21">Jdg 20:19-21</reference>. They renew the battle next day, and are discomfited with the loss of eighteen thousand men, <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.22-Jdg.20.25">Jdg 20:22-25</reference>. They weep, fast, and pray, and offer sacrifices; and again inquire of the Lord, who promises to deliver Benjamin into their hands, <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.26-Jdg.20.28">Jdg 20:26-28</reference>. They concert plans, attack the Benjamites, and rout them, killing twenty-five thousand one hundred men, and destroy the city of Gibeah, <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.29-Jdg.20.37">Jdg 20:29-37</reference>. A recapitulation of the different actions in which they were killed, <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.38-Jdg.20.46">Jdg 20:38-46</reference>. Six hundred men escape to the rock Rimmon, <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.47">Jdg 20:47</reference>. The Israelites destroy all the cities of the Benjamites, <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.48">Jdg 20:48</reference>. <div eID="gen9189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9190" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen9190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9191" type="x-p"/> Unto the Lord in Mizpeh - This city was situated on the confines of Judah and Benjamin, and is sometimes attributed to the one, sometimes to the other. It seems that there was a place here in which the Lord was consulted, as well as at Shiloh; in 1 Maccabees 3:46, we read, In Maspha was the place where they prayed aforetime in Israel. These two passages cast light on each other. Some think that Shiloh is meant, because the ark was there; but the phrase before the Lord may signify no more than meeting in the name of God to consult him, and make prayer and supplication. Wherever God's people are, there is God himself; and it ever was true, that wherever two or three were assembled in his name, he was in the midst of them.
entries.da2a231ae2b1ba11db59966b5b637c8edebec4d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen9191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9192" type="x-p"/> The chief of all the people - The corners פנות pinnoth; for as the corner-stones are the strength of the walls, so are the chiefs the strength of the people. Hence Christ is called the chief corner-stone. <div eID="gen9192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9193" type="x-p"/> In the assembly of the people of God - The Septuagint translate, And all the tribes of Israel stood up before the face of the Lord, εν εκκλησιᾳ του λαου του Θεου, in the Church of the people of God. Here was a Church, though there was no priest; for, as Tertullian says, Ubi tres, ecclesia est, licet laici; "Wheresoever three are gathered together in the name of the Lord, there is a Church, although there be none but the laity."
entries.f0f3de37aa3adfb141400a0f5bb5e0713ed11a6b: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen9193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9194" type="x-p"/> Tell us, how was this wickedness? - They had heard before, by the messengers he sent with the fragments of his wife's body; but they wish to hear it, in full council, from himself.
entries.d69c8fe22811c29254e2ae0239432e8262070b24: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen9194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9195" type="x-p"/> We will not any of us go to his tent - We will have satisfaction for this wickedness before we return home.
entries.1a40efdd467d361f695eb786b09f79976f77beb8: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen9195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9196" type="x-p"/> Ten men of a hundred - Expecting that they might have a long contest, they provide suttlers for the camp; and it is probable that they chose these tenths by lot.
entries.d88fa212cd3cec9e9dd7bf9e0ce9c7dfe45aafe5: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen9196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9197" type="x-p"/> Deliver us the men - Nothing could be fairer than this. They wish only to make the murderers answerable for their guilt. <div eID="gen9197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9198" type="x-p"/> Benjamin would not hearken - Thus making their whole tribe partakers of the guilt of the men of Gibeah. By not delivering up those bad men, they in effect said: "We will stand by them in what they have done, and would have acted the same part had we been present." This proves that the whole tribe was excessively depraved.
entries.772e48212f43532768570540f97f41257bea27f5: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen9198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9199" type="x-p"/> Twenty and six thousand - Some copies of the Septuagint have twenty-three thousand, others twenty-five thousand. The Vulgate has this latter number; the Complutensian Polyglot and Josephus have the same.
entries.b570b5aed0faefb8de15e7c8924a16be3ba78cf6: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen9199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9200" type="x-p"/> Left-handed - They were ambidexters - could use the right hand and the left with equal ease and effect. See the note on <reference osisRef="Jdg.3.15">Jdg 3:15</reference>. <div eID="gen9200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9201" type="x-p"/> Could sling stones at a hair - and not miss - ולא יחטא velo yachati, and not sin: και ουκ εξαμαρτανοντες; Sept. Here we have the true import of the term sin; it signifies simply to miss the mark, and is well translated in the New Testament by ἁμαρτανω, from α, negative, and μαρπτω, to hit the mark. Men miss the mark of true happiness in aiming at sensual gratifications; which happiness is to be found only in the possession and enjoyment of the favor of God, from whom their passions continually lead them. He alone hits the mark, and ceases from sin, who attains to God through Christ Jesus. <div eID="gen9201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9202" type="x-p"/> It is worthy of remark that the Persian khuta kerden, which literally signifies to sin or mistake, is used by the Mohammedans to express to miss the mark. <div eID="gen9202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9203" type="x-p"/> The sling was a very ancient warlike instrument, and, in the hands of those who were skilled in the use of it, it produced astonishing effects. The inhabitants of the isles called Baleares, now Majorca and Minorca, were the most celebrated slingers of antiquity. They did not permit their children to break their fast till they had struck down the bread they were to eat from the top of a pole, or some distant eminence. They had their name Baleares from the Greek word βαλλειν to dart, cast, or throw. <div eID="gen9203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9204" type="x-p"/> Concerning the velocity of the ball out of the sling, there are strange and almost incredible things told by the ancients. The leaden ball, when thus projected, is said to have melted in its course. So Ovid, Met. lib. ii.. ver. 726. <div eID="gen9204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9205" type="x-p"/> Obstupuit forma Jove natus: et aethere pendens <div eID="gen9205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9206" type="x-p"/> Non secus exarsit, quam cum balearica plumbum <div eID="gen9206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9207" type="x-p"/> Funda jacit; volat illud, et incandescit eundo; <div eID="gen9207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9208" type="x-p"/> Et, quos non habuit, sub nubibus invenit ignes. <div eID="gen9208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9209" type="x-p"/> Hermes was fired as in the clouds he hung; <div eID="gen9209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9210" type="x-p"/> So the cold bullet that, with fury slung <div eID="gen9210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9211" type="x-p"/> From Balearic engines, mounts on high, <div eID="gen9211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9212" type="x-p"/> Glows in the whirl, and burns along the sky. <div eID="gen9212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9213" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen9213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9214" type="x-p"/> This is not a poetic fiction; Seneca, the philosopher, in lib. iii. Quaest. Natural., c. 57, says the same thing: Sic liquescit excussa glans funda, et adtritu aeris velut igne distillat; "Thus the ball projected from the sling melts, and is liquefied by the friction of the air, as if it were exposed to the action of fire." I have often, by the sudden and violent compression of the air, produced fire; and by this alone inflamed tinder, and lighted a match. Vegetius de Re Militari, lib. ii., cap. 23, tells us that slingers could in general hit the mark at six hundred feet distance. Funditores scopas-pro signo ponebant; ita ut Sexcentos Pedes removerentur a signo-signum saepius tangerent. These things render credible what is spoken here of the Benjamite slingers.
entries.b64db49075826d8c7e23a95ca4e0365b94d4e1ff: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen9214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9215" type="x-p"/> Went up to the house of God - Some think that a deputation was sent from Shiloh, where Phinehas the high priest was, to inquire, not concerning the expediency of the war, nor of its success, but which of the tribes should begin the attack. Having so much right on their side, they had no doubt of the justice of their cause. Having such a superiority of numbers, they had no doubt of success. See the note on <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.1">Jdg 20:1</reference>. <div eID="gen9215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9216" type="x-p"/> And the Lord said, Judah - But he did not say that they should conquer.
entries.83b912077e0fd98ad52478e77147cb92ef421328: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen9216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9217" type="x-p"/> Destroyed down to the ground - twenty-two thousand men - That is, so many were left dead on the field of battle.
entries.14eb8911b045a141d9beea085a54cdaf73d34339: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen9217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9218" type="x-p"/> Go up against him - It appears most evident that the Israelites did not seek the protection of God. They trusted in the goodness of their cause and in the multitude of their army. God humbled them, and delivered them into the hands of their enemies, and showed them that the race was not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong.
entries.4c373ba4dd8d3bd277c438a2f26c11796289da46: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen9218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9219" type="x-p"/> And wept - Had they humbled themselves, fasted, and prayed, and offered sacrifices at first, they had not been discomfited. <div eID="gen9219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9220" type="x-p"/> And fasted that day until even - This is the first place where fasting is mentioned as a religious ceremony, or as a means of obtaining help from God. And in this case, and many since, it has been powerfully effectual. At present it is but little used; a strong proof that self-denial is wearing out of fashion.
entries.43e81da037a3af1d9bdd2e94a80b42553befee13: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen9220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9221" type="x-p"/> Phinehas, the son of Eleazar - This was the same Phinehas who is mentioned <reference osisRef="Num.25.7">Num 25:7</reference>, and consequently these transactions must have taken place shortly after the death of Joshua.
entries.efea99d3a8a90c1875354ac336308ce3c29616be: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen9221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9222" type="x-p"/> Israel set liers in wait - Though God had promised them success, they knew they could expect it only in the use of the proper means. They used all prudent precaution, and employed all their military skill.
entries.a4fef151ce38e23f595f8913e8c8327df26e9a8f: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen9222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9223" type="x-p"/> Let us - draw them from the city - They had two reasons for this: <div eID="gen9223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9224" type="x-p"/> 1. They had placed an ambuscade behind Gibeah, which was to enter and burn the city as soon as the Benjamites had left it. <div eID="gen9224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9225" type="x-p"/> 2. It would seem that the slingers, by being within the city and its fortifications, had great advantage against the Israelites by their slings, whom they could not annoy with their swords, unless they got them to the plain country.
entries.e1c2749d1e876a41333e8517d25b39dd21e18e6d: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen9225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9226" type="x-p"/> Put themselves in array at Baal-tamar - The Israelites seem to have divided their army into three divisions; one was at Baal-tamar, a second behind the city in ambush, and the third skirmished with the Benjamites before Gibeah.
entries.e359fe995a68823d57cce78dbb947760355edd0e: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen9226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9227" type="x-p"/> Twenty and five thousand and a hundred - As the Benjamites consisted only of twenty-six thousand and seven hundred slingers; or, as the Vulgate, Septuagint, and others read, twenty-five thousand, which is most probably the true reading; then the whole of the Benjamites were cut to pieces, except six hundred men, who we are informed fled to the rock Rimmon, where they fortified themselves.
entries.049937beae21743433c42f0b2259bde98e3b2e38: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen9227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9228" type="x-p"/> Now there was an appointed sign - From this verse to the end of the chapter we have the details of the same operations which are mentioned, in a general way, in the preceding part of the chapter.
entries.501c4087f9770a4d56ec6e90548e9401550724c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 45</hi> <div eID="gen9228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9229" type="x-p"/> Unto the rock of Rimmon - This was some strong place, but where situated is not known. Here they maintained themselves four months, and it was by these alone that the tribe of Benjamin was preserved from utter extermination. See the following chapter, Judges 21 (note). <div eID="gen9229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9230" type="x-p"/> It is scarcely possible to imagine any thing more horrid than the indiscriminate and relentless slaughter of both innocent and guilty mentioned in this chapter. The crime of the men of Gibeah was great, but there was no adequate cause for this relentless extermination of a whole tribe. There was neither justice nor judgment in this case; they were on all sides brutal, cruel, and ferocious: and no wonder; there was no king in Israel - no effective civil government, and every man did what was right in his own eyes. There was no proper leader; no man that had authority and influence to repress the disorderly workings of the pell-mell mob.  <chapter eID="Judg.20"/> <div eID="gen9230" type="x-p"/>

entries.aee3e6749f57d9b77f5397cba78fec047f5429ff: Jdg 20:1-2 <hi type="italic">Decree of the Congregation concerning Gibeah</hi>. - Jdg 20:1, Jdg 20:2. All the Israelites went out (rose up from their dwelling-places) to assemble together as a congregation like one man; all the tribes from Dan, the northern boundary of the land (i.e., Dan-laish, Jdg 18:29), to Beersheba, the most southerly town of Canaan (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.21.31">Gen 21:31</reference>), and the land of Gilead, i.e., the inhabitants of the land to the east of the Jordan, “<hi type="italic">to Jehovah at Mizpeh</hi>” in Benjamin, i.e., the present <hi type="italic">Nebi-samwil</hi>, in the neighbourhood of Kirjath-jearim, on the western border of the tribe of Benjamin (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.18.26">Jos 18:26</reference>). It by no means follows with certainty from the expression “to <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>,” that there was a sanctuary at Mizpeh, or that the ark of the covenant was taken thither, but simply that the meeting took place in the sight of Jehovah, or that the congregation assembled together to hold a judicial court, which they held in the name of Jehovah, analogous to the expression <hi type="italic">el</hi>-<hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.6">Exo 21:6</reference>; Exo 22:7. It was not essential to a judicial proceeding that the ark should be present. At this assembly the <hi type="italic">pinnoth</hi> (the corner-pillars) <hi type="italic">of the whole nation presented themselves</hi>, i.e., the heads and fathers as the supports of the congregation or of the sate organism (vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.38">1Sa 14:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.13">Isa 19:13</reference>), even of all the tribes of Israel four hundred thousand men on foot, drawing the sword, i.e., armed foot soldiers ready for battle.
entries.ed080ca74abe021d0806dcb9b5c01f3645f69605: Jdg 20:3 <div eID="gen3503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3504" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">The Benjaminites heard that the children of Israel</hi> (the rest of the Israelites, the eleven tribes) <hi type="italic">had come up to Mizpeh;</hi>” but they themselves were not found there. This follows from the fact that nothing is said about the Benjaminites coming, and still more clearly from Jdg 20:13, where it is stated that the assembled tribes sent men to the Benjaminites, after holding their deliberations and forming their resolutions, to call them to account for the crime that had been committed in the midst of them. Consequently the question with which the whole affair was opened, “<hi type="italic">Say, how did this wicked deed take place?</hi>” is not to be regarded as addressed to the two parties, the inhabitants of Gibeah of the Benjaminites <hi type="italic">and</hi> the Levite (<hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi>), but as a summons to all who were assembled to relate what any one knew respecting the occurrence.
entries.f273d508942f5a0d2cb62bedee137b115e9534c9: Jdg 20:4-7 <div eID="gen3504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3505" type="x-p"/> Then the Levite, the husband of the murdered woman, described the whole affair. הגּבעה בּעלי, the owners or citizens of Gibeah (see at Jdg 9:2). “<hi type="italic">Me they intended to kill:</hi>” the Levite draws this conclusion from what had happened to his wife; the men of Gibeah had not expressed any such intention in Jdg 19:22. “<hi type="italic">All the country</hi> (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. field) <hi type="italic">of the inheritance of Israel,</hi>” i.e., all the land of the Israelites. זמּה is applied to the vice of lewdness, as in <reference osisRef="Lev.18.17">Lev 18:17</reference>, which was to be punished with death. וגו לכם הבוּ, “<hi type="italic">give yourselves</hi> (לכם as<hi type="italic">dat. comm</hi>.) <hi type="italic">word and counsel here,</hi>” i.e., make up your minds and pass sentence (vid., <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.20">2Sa 16:20</reference>). הלם, here, where you are all assembled together.
entries.5eb8059a287d33c2f288359a06544ea74e64682a: Jdg 20:8-10 <div eID="gen3505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3506" type="x-p"/> Then all the people rose up as one man, saying, “<hi type="italic">We will not any of us go into his tent, neither will we any of us return to his house,</hi>” sc., till this crime is punished. The sentence follows in Jdg 20:9 : “<hi type="italic">This is the thing that we will do,</hi>” i.e., this is the way in which we will treat Gibeah: “<hi type="italic">against it by lot</hi>” (sc., we will act). The <hi type="italic">Syriac</hi> gives the sense correctly - We will cast lots upon it; but the lxx quite erroneously supply ἀναβησόμεθα (we will go up); and in accordance with this, many expositors connect the words with Jdg 20:10 in the following sense: “We will choose one man out of every ten by lot, to supply the army with the necessary provision during the expedition.” This is quite a mistake, because in this way a subordinate point, which only comes into consideration in connection with the execution of the sentence, would be made the chief point, and the sentence itself would not be given at all. The words “<hi type="italic">against it by lot</hi>” contain the resolution that was formed concerning the sinful town, and have all the enigmatical brevity of judicial sentences, and are to be explained from the course laid down in the Mosaic law with regard to the Canaanites, who were to be exterminated, and their land divided by lot among the Israelites. Consequently the meaning is simply this: “Let us proceed with the lot against Gibeah,” i.e., let us deal with it as with the towns of the Canaanites, conquer it, lay it in ashes, and distribute its territory by lot. In Jdg 20:10 a subordinate circumstance is mentioned, which was necessary to enable them to carry out the resolution that had been made. As the assembled congregation had determined to keep together for the purpose of carrying on war (Jdg 20:8), it was absolutely necessary that resources should be provided for those who were actively engaged in the war. For this purpose they chose one man in every ten “<hi type="italic">to fetch provision for the people,</hi>” לבואם לעשׁות, “<hi type="italic">that they might do on their coming to Gibeah of Benjamin according to all the folly which had been done in Israel,</hi>” i.e., might punish the wickedness in Gibeah as it deserved.
entries.3c93cb6d36acfb8cfbf4e3d2e57e44fac4df5f86: Jdg 20:11 <div eID="gen3506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3507" type="x-p"/> Thus the men of Israel assembled together against Gibeah, united as one man. חברים, <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. as comrades, simply serves to strengthen the expression “as one man.” With this remark, which indicates briefly the carrying out of the resolution that was adopted, the account of the meeting of the congregation is brought to a close; but the actual progress of the affair is really anticipated, inasmuch as what is related in Jdg 20:12-21 preceded the expedition in order of time.
entries.437827d7d67963db6a0ce9d348b0462b1bc0af0f: Jdg 20:12-13 <div eID="gen3507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3508" type="x-p"/> Before the tribes of Israel entered upon the war, they sent men to all the tribes of Benjamin, who were to demand that the culprits in Gibeah should be given up to be punished, that the evil might thus be exterminated from Israel, according to the law in <reference osisRef="Deut.22.22">Deu 22:22</reference> as compared with Jdg 13:6 and Jdg 17:12. “<hi type="italic">The tribes of Benjamin</hi>” are the same as “the families of Benjamin:” the historian pictured to himself the different divisions of the tribe of Benjamin as warlike powers about to carry on a war with the other tribes of Israel. The word <hi type="italic">shebet</hi> (tribe) is used in a different way in Num 4:18. But the Benjaminites would not hearken to the voice of their brethren, the other tribes of Israel. The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> (sons of Benjamin) is a needless alteration, since <hi type="italic">Benjamin</hi> may be construed with the plural as a collective term. By refusing this just demand on the part of the other tribes, the Benjaminites took the side of the culprits in Gibeah, and compelled the congregation to make war upon the whole tribe.
entries.5b29f4d7d0774949165d819def5e25fd1833d1ae: Jdg 20:14-16 <div eID="gen3508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3509" type="x-p"/> Both sides now made their preparations. The Benjaminites assembled together at Gibeah out of their different towns, and “<hi type="italic">were mustered 26,000 men drawing the sword, beside the inhabitants of Gibeah they were mustered, 700 picked men</hi>” (הגפּקדוּ, with the reduplication dropped, like the <hi type="italic">Hothpael</hi> in Num 1:47). “<hi type="italic">Out of all this people there were 700 picked men, lamed in the right hand, all these </hi>(were) <hi type="italic">slinging with a stone</hi> (hitting) <hi type="italic">at a hair’s breadth without fail</hi>.” These statement are not quite clear.
